newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Top N.Korean defector to meet Seoul journalists.
newsitem.headline: Top N.Korean defector to meet Seoul journalists.

text.p: Hwang Jang-yop, the highest-ranking North Korean ever to defect to South Korea, plans a news conference next week, intelligence officials in Seoul said.
South Korea's Agency for National Security Planning (NSP), formerly known as the Korean Central Intelligence Agency, has completed an investigation into Hwang's defection, they said on Wednesday.
Diplomats have said Hwang could give an insight into the state of the reclusive nation's government and military as it slides towards famine after being hit by devastating floods in 1995 and 1996.

Hwang had planned his news conference for Friday, when the NSP was to announce its findings. An NSP spokesman said this announcement had been postponed because opposition lawmakers were due to deliver their policy speeches on Friday and were concerned about losing publicity.
"It will be delayed by about a week," the spokesman said. "Mr Hwang's news conference will also be delayed accordingly."

Hwang, the architect of North Korea's guiding ideology of self-reliance, or "juche", sought asylum at South Korea's Beijing consulate in February and arrived in Seoul in April after more than two months in China and the Philippines.
Hwang's planned news conference will now come shortly after Tuesday's third anniversary of the death of North Korea's "Great Leader", Kim Il-sung.

Analysts said the anniversary, marking the end of the traditional three-year mourning period, would clear the way for Kim's son, Kim Jong-il, to be formally anointed as general secretary of the ruling Workers' Party and state president.
The two posts have been left vacant since the death of the senior Kim.

In an arrival statement last April, Hwang warned that the younger Kim was looking for an opportunity to strike against the South and that he came to the South to avert another war on the Korean peninsula.
Communist North Korea and the capitalist South, split at the end of World War Two, fought a mutually devastating war in 1950-53 that ended in a truce, not a peace pact.
The North formally agreed on Monday to a meeting on August 5 in New York of senior officials from the two Koreas, the United States and China to arrange four-nation peace talks.
The four-nation talks are aimed at thrashing out a permanent peace settlement to replace the fraying 1953 truce agreement.
